items.name: free vector space functor k[-]: Set -> Vect_k, left adjoint to the underlying-set functor
items.statement_summary: Chapter-opening unnumbered construction. The underlying-set functor U: Vect_k -> Vect_k's target Set is forgetful on a vector space; reversing it, the free vector space k[S] on a set S has S as a basis, its elements being finite formal sums k_1 s_1 + ... + k_n s_n with k_i in k, s_i in S, n >= 0 (footnote 1: precisely, a finitely supported function S -> k). The assignment is functorial: f: S -> T induces the linear map k[f]: k[S] -> k[T] determined on basis elements, giving k[-]: Set -> Vect_k. Its universal property is stated as k[-] being LEFT ADJOINT to U: linear maps k[S] -> V correspond naturally to functions S -> U(V), which by the Yoneda lemma determines the action of k[-] on maps. Accompanying unnumbered assertion (footnote 2): U: Vect_k -> Set has no right adjoint, so no competing 'cofree' construction exists.

items.name: adjunction (adjunctions I) — hom-set definition
items.statement_summary: An adjunction consists of a pair of functors F: C -> D and G: D -> C together with a specified isomorphism D(Fc,d) = C(c,Gd) for each c in C and d in D that is natural in BOTH variables. F is called left adjoint to G and G right adjoint to F. Morphisms f-sharp: Fc -> d and f-flat: c -> Gd corresponding under the bijection are called adjunct, or transposes of each other. The naturality clause means the isomorphisms assemble into a natural isomorphism of the two hom-bifunctors C^op x D -> SET obtained by restricting D(-,-) along F x id and C(-,-) along id x G (possibly valued in a larger set-theoretic universe).

items.name: naturality of adjoint transposition as commuting-square correspondence
items.statement_summary: Let F: C -> D and G: D -> C be equipped with specified isomorphisms D(Fc,d) = C(c,Gd) for all c in C and d in D (not assumed natural). Then naturality of this collection is EQUIVALENT to the assertion that for all morphisms h: c' -> c in C, k: d -> d' in D, f-sharp: Fc -> d, g-sharp: Fc' -> d', the square in D with sides Fh, f-sharp, g-sharp, k commutes if and only if the transposed square in C with sides h, f-flat, g-flat, Gk commutes. (Proof deferred to Exercise 4.1.i.) The two naturality directions separately say: the transpose of k . f-sharp is Gk . f-flat, and the transpose of f-sharp . Fh is f-flat . h.

items.name: Notation 4.1.5 — the turnstile notation for adjoints
items.statement_summary: Notation (numbered environment of kind Notation). Following Kan, a turnstile designates an adjoint pair: the expressions F -| G and G |- F, and each of four decorated bidirectional diagrams between C and D carrying the symbol 'perp' between the two arrows, all assert that F: C -> D is left adjoint to G: D -> C. The notation is intended for contexts involving several adjoint functors at once.

items.name: discrete -| forgetful -| indiscrete for Top -> Set
items.statement_summary: The forgetful functor U: Top -> Set admits BOTH a left and a right adjoint. The left adjoint sends a set S to the discrete space D(S), characterized by the universal property that any function S -> U(T) is continuous as a map D(S) -> T; the right adjoint sends S to the indiscrete space I(S), characterized by: any function U(T) -> S is continuous as a map T -> I(S). The natural isomorphisms Top(D(S),T) = Set(S,U(T)) and Set(U(T),S) = Top(T,I(S)) exhibit D -| U -| I.

items.name: adjoint triple
items.statement_summary: Unnumbered definition made in running prose: when three functors F, G, H define a pair of adjunctions F -| G and G -| H, this data collectively is called an adjoint triple.

items.name: (monotone) Galois connection; lower and upper adjoint
items.statement_summary: Unnumbered definition made in running prose: an adjunction between preorders is called a (monotone) Galois connection. Recalling from Exercise 1.3.ii that functors between preorders A and B are exactly order-preserving functions, an adjunction F -| G between order-preserving F: A -> B and G: B -> A asserts precisely that Fa <= b if and only if a <= Gb, for all a in A and b in B. In this context F is called the lower adjoint and G the upper adjoint.

items.name: ceiling -| inclusion -| floor for Z -> R
items.statement_summary: The inclusion of posets Z -> R with the usual ordering has both adjoints, given by the ceiling and floor functions. For an integer n and real r, n <= r if and only if n <= floor(r), so floor: R -> Z is right adjoint to the inclusion; dually r <= n if and only if ceiling(r) <= n, so ceiling: R -> Z is left adjoint to the inclusion. Hence an adjoint triple ceiling -| i -| floor between Z and R.

items.name: direct image -| inverse image -| dual image for a function of sets
items.statement_summary: For a function f: A -> B, the powersets PA and PB are posets ordered by inclusion. The direct image f_* : PA -> PB and inverse image f^{-1}: PB -> PA satisfy: for A' subset A and B' subset B, f(A') subset B' if and only if A' subset f^{-1}(B'); i.e. f_* -| f^{-1}. The inverse image has a further right adjoint f_! carrying A' subset A to the set of elements of B whose fibres lie entirely inside A', characterized by B' subset f_!(A') if and only if f^{-1}(B') subset A'. Together these give an adjoint triple f_* -| f^{-1} -| f_! between PA and PB.

items.name: quantifiers as adjoints: exists_X -| Delta_X -| forall_X
items.statement_summary: A predicate (propositional function) on X is a function p: X -> Omega where Omega := {bottom, top} is the set of truth values, made a poset category by the single non-identity morphism bottom <= top; Omega^X carries the pointwise order (p <= q iff p(x) implies q(x) for all x). Universal and existential quantification define functors forall_X, exists_X: Omega^X -> Omega by: forall_X p = top iff p(x) = top for all x in X, and exists_X p = top iff p(x) = top for some x. With the constant functor Delta_X: Omega -> Omega^X these form an adjoint triple exists_X -| Delta_X -| forall_X.

items.name: the family of free -| forgetful adjunctions (fourteen instances)
items.statement_summary: A large family of adjunctions F -| U: A <-> S where U is forgetful and F free; when a universal object of type A can be built on an object of type S and this construction is left adjoint to a forgetful functor, the word 'free' is used for 'universal'. Fourteen listed forgetful functors admitting left adjoints: (i) U: Set_* -> Set, free pointed set X_+ = X + {X}; (ii) U: Monoid -> Set, free monoid the set of finite lists of elements of X; (iii) U: Ring -> Ab forgetting multiplication, free ring on an abelian group A the direct sum of tensor powers A^{tensor n}, n >= 0; (iv) U: Ab -> Set, free abelian group Z[X] = direct sum over X of Z; (v) U: _R Mod -> Set, free R-module R[X] = direct sum over X of R (specializing to the free k-vector space of the chapter introduction); (vi) U: Ring -> Set, free ring the free monoid on the free abelian group, obtained by composing left adjoints (Proposition 4.3.4); (vii) U: CRing -> Set, free commutative ring = polynomials over Z in the elements of X; (viii) (-)^x: Ring -> Group carrying a ring to its group of units, whose left adjoint is the group ring Z[G]; (ix) U: Group -> Set, free group (see Examples 4.2.4 and 4.7.6); (x) I: Ab -> CMonoid, left adjoint the group completion / Grothendieck group Gr(M,+,0) = (M x M) modulo (a,b) ~ (a',b') iff a + b' + c = a' + b + c for some c; (xi) I: Group -> Monoid, left adjoint the group completion of a monoid; (xii) restriction of scalars phi^*: _S Mod -> _R Mod along phi: R -> S, whose left adjoint S tensor_R - is extension of scalars; (xiii) U: _R Mod -> Ab forgetting scalar multiplication, the special case of (xii) for the unique Z -> R; (xiv) phi^*: Set^{BG} -> Set^{BH} along a group homomorphism phi: H -> G, whose left adjoint is called induction. Each of these is a monadic adjunction (subject of section 5.5).

items.name: Frobenius reciprocity: induction -| restriction -| coinduction
items.statement_summary: Generalizing Example 4.1.10(xiv): for any complete and cocomplete category C and any group homomorphism phi: H -> G, the restriction functor phi^*: C^{BG} -> C^{BH} admits both a left and a right adjoint (proved in Example 6.2.9). For a subgroup inclusion H subset G the left adjoint is called induction ind^G_H and the right adjoint coinduction coind^G_H, so ind -| res -| coind. Taking C = Vect_k, the adjunction ind^G_H -| res^G_H between H-representations and G-representations is Frobenius reciprocity.

items.name: the forgetful functors out of Field admit no adjoints
items.statement_summary: None of the functors Field -> Ring, Field -> Ab, Field -(-)^x-> Ab, Field -> Set that forget algebraic structure on fields admits a left or a right adjoint. Reason given: the target categories admit maps from Z to fields of every characteristic, but there are no field homomorphisms between fields of differing characteristic, so no value for a hypothetical left adjoint at Z can be defined; a similar argument rules out right adjoints.

items.name: free category on a quiver
items.statement_summary: The forgetful functor U: Cat -> Quiver admits a left adjoint F defining the free category on a quiver. A quiver Q is a set V of vertices, a set A of arrows, and functions s,t: A -> V giving source and target. The free category F(Q) has V as objects; its morphisms are finite directed paths of edges, with the nullary paths serving as identities and composition given by concatenation. The adjunction supplies a natural bijection between functors F(Q) -> C and quiver morphisms Q -> U(C); such data is exactly a diagram in C with no commutativity requirements, uniquely determined by the images of the vertices and arrows of Q. These images are the atomic arrows of F(Q), those admitting no non-trivial factorization; e.g. the category omega is free on the quiver with vertices the natural numbers and edges n -> n+1, so an omega-indexed diagram is specified by the images of the atomic arrows alone.

items.name: arbitrarily long finite chains of adjoints between ordinal categories
items.statement_summary: For n >= 0 let n+1 denote the ordinal category freely generated by the quiver 0 -> 1 -> ... -> n. For 0 <= i <= n there is an injective functor d^i: n -> n+1, the unique functor missing the object i from the image; for 0 <= i < n there is a surjective functor s^i: n+1 -> n for which i in n is the unique object with two preimages. These functors form a sequence of 2n+1 adjoints d^n -| s^{n-1} -| d^{n-1} -| s^{n-2} -| ... -| s^1 -| d^1 -| s^0 -| d^0 between n and n+1, proving that arbitrarily long finite sequences of adjoint functors exist.

items.name: maximal subgroupoid and category of fractions as adjoints to Groupoid -> Cat
items.statement_summary: The inclusion Groupoid -> Cat admits both a left and a right adjoint. The right adjoint sends a category to its maximal subgroupoid (Lemma 1.1.14): since functors preserve isomorphisms, any functor from a groupoid G -> C factors uniquely through the maximal subgroupoid of C. The left adjoint formally inverts all morphisms, producing the category of fractions; for C it is constructed as a quotient of the free category on the quiver obtained by gluing the quiver underlying C to the quiver underlying C^op along the common discrete subcategory ob C. Its objects are those of C and its morphisms are finite zig-zags of morphisms of C, subject to relations equating the zig-zags a -f-> b <-f- a and b <-f- a -f-> b with identities. (Reference: Bor94a, section 5.2.)
